ai-infrastructure/learning-cxx.body:
## Overview

This personal fork follows the LearningInfiniTensor C++ curriculum. It contains exercise implementations covering core language features and standard-library facilities, including object lifetimes, templates, containers, and smart pointers.

## Implementation

The historical [C++ exercise commit](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/learning-cxx/commit/06ac0678f2395ad76cab73f945d9cbd3ac01d930) changes 34 exercise source files. For example, the accumulation exercise uses `std::accumulate` to calculate a tensor's byte size. These changes belong to the learning fork; they are not presented as accepted upstream contributions.

## Verification

The source README describes the xmake build and exercise runner. Some verification assertions in the smart-pointer exercise are currently commented out, and generated build files were included in the historical commit. Restoring those checks and cleaning the generated artifacts remain follow-up work; the repository is not described as having passed every exercise.

## Source

[GitHub repository](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/learning-cxx)

meta.title: llkdocker
meta.excerpt: A Go implementation that explores container isolation, resource controls, layered filesystems, and bind-mounted volumes through separate Linux exercises.

ai-infrastructure/llkdocker.body: ## Background What happens between a container command and the process running inside it? llkdocker studies that path in Go, following the *Write Your Own Docker* learning approach on Ubuntu 22.04. Separate directories preserve successive exercises, making it possible to examine isolation, filesystems, and resource controls without navigating a full container engine. ## Implementation The [`volume_docker` exercise](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkdocker/tree/main/volume_docker) brings several mechanisms together: - **Process isolation:** the parent starts an `init` child using UTS, PID, mount, network, and IPC namespace flags. - **Parent–child coordination:** an inherited pipe carries the requested command after the parent assigns the child to a cgroup. - **Root filesystem:** BusyBox supplies the lower filesystem; OverlayFS combines lower, upper, work, and merged directories. The child changes its root with `pivot_root` and mounts `/proc` and `/dev`. - **Resources and storage:** command options feed memory, CPU, and cpuset settings into cgroup handlers; `-v` maps a host directory through a bind mount. - **Lifecycle:** the parent waits for the child, then calls volume, overlay, and cgroup cleanup routines. ## Design and learning scope The progression from `namespace` and `run_docker` to `pipe_docker`, `pivotroot_docker`, `overlayfs_docker`, and `volume_docker` exposes how the pieces fit together. Isolation and resource allocation remain visible as separate mechanisms. The code also makes filesystem preparation and process cleanup explicit, useful places to study failure paths and ownership of host resources. ## Environment and use The module declares Go 1.18 and uses `urfave/cli` and Logrus. Execution requires Linux features, mount permissions, a suitable cgroup configuration, and the BusyBox root filesystem. Paths under `/home/llk/Desktop/docker/src/volume_docker` are embedded in the source and must be adapted to the local workspace. Start by reading [`command.go`](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkdocker/blob/main/volume_docker/command.go) for supported flags, then follow [`container/run.go`](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkdocker/blob/main/volume_docker/container/run.go) and [`container/init.go`](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkdocker/blob/main/volume_docker/container/init.go). ## Development history [Browse the staged exercises](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkdocker/tree/main) · [View repository commits](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkdocker/commits/main/)

meta.title: MagicSkills
meta.excerpt: A shared skill library for AI agents, with reusable collections, AGENTS.md synchronization, and CLI/Python integration.

ai-infrastructure/magicskills.body: ## The problem A team using several agents can accumulate many copies of the same `SKILL.md` directory. Updates then need to be repeated, each agent's available capabilities become harder to track, and framework migrations introduce another integration layer. MagicSkills, developed in [Narwhal-Lab](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab), gives those reusable instructions and supporting files a common management workflow. The practical goal is to maintain a skill once, select an appropriate working set for each agent, and connect that set to different runtimes. The project includes examples for agent applications and frameworks such as Codex, Cursor, LangChain, and CrewAI. See the [project overview](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills#overview-en) for the supported integration patterns. ## How the pieces fit **Skill discovery.** A skill is a directory containing `SKILL.md`. The implementation records its path, description, and source, allowing the content to stay in ordinary files that can be inspected and versioned. **Collection composition.** A `Skills` instance selects the capabilities needed by one workflow. Several collections can reference the same installed directory. Lookup accepts names or explicit paths, which resolves ambiguity when two directories share a name. These operations live in the [collection implementation](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills/blob/main/src/magicskills/type/skills.py). **Persistence and integration.** `REGISTRY` stores collection configuration and path references in `~/.magicskills/collections.json`; it does not duplicate the complete skill contents. Synchronization generates the skills section of `AGENTS.md`. Frameworks can instead call the collection's list, read, and execution interface through Python or the CLI. The [registry implementation](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills/blob/main/src/magicskills/type/skillsregistry.py) and [Python API guide](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills/blob/main/doc/python-api.md) explain these boundaries. ## Try the documented workflow The following example uses the repository's included C-to-AST skill and a fresh collection name. It follows the [CLI documentation](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills/blob/main/doc/cli.md); Python 3.10–3.13 and Git are required. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills.git cd MagicSkills python -m pip install -e . magicskills install skill_template -t ./demo-skills magicskills addskills portfolio_demo --skill-list c_2_ast --agent-md-path ./demo-agent/AGENTS.md magicskills syncskills portfolio_demo magicskills skill-tool listskill --name portfolio_demo ``` Review the synchronization prompt to write the generated file. The final command lists the selected skill; reading its instructions and running its parser are separate steps. The [sample skill](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills/tree/main/skill_template/c_2_ast) provides those files. Execution uses the current working directory, so an integration must choose its working directory explicitly. ## Development history and writing The [commit history](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills/commits/main/) and [pull requests](https://github.com/Narwhal-Lab/MagicSkills/pulls?q=is%3Apr) provide the public implementation record. For a longer explanation of the skill reuse model, see my [MagicSkills technical article]({{ '/posts/csdn-159395734/' | relative_url }}).

meta.title: glibc-chunk-poc-basic
meta.excerpt: Small C examples and allocator notes covering glibc heap behavior, bin manipulation, and version-specific exploitation techniques.

endpoint-security/glibc-chunk-poc-basic.body:
## Background

glibc allocator behavior becomes easier to reason about when a technique is reduced to a small allocation sequence. This repository collects C proof-of-concept programs alongside notes on chunk metadata, allocator checks, and debugging. The README credits the existing heap exploitation material used throughout the collection.

## Implementation and coverage

The source tree organizes examples by technique, including `unlink`, fastbin double free, unsorted and large bins, overlapping chunks, and tcache manipulation. Further directories explore IO structures, exit handling, and related control-flow targets.

Two compact examples illustrate the approach:

| Example | What the code makes visible |
| --- | --- |
| [`fastbin_double_free/2.23.c`](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/glibc-chunk-poc-basic/blob/main/fastbin_double_free/2.23.c) | A repeated free sequence and subsequent allocations, with an address comparison at the end. |
| [`tcache_poisoning/2.27.c`](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/glibc-chunk-poc-basic/blob/main/tcache_poisoning/2.27.c) | Modification of a freed entry followed by allocations and printed destination addresses. |

The examples keep the allocation sequence close to the behavior being studied. This supports reading allocator source and inspecting memory in a debugger, rather than hiding the mechanism behind a larger target program.

## Environment and reproduction

Version labels are part of the examples' context. A program written for glibc 2.23 or 2.27 should be examined with the intended allocator and dynamic loader; behavior on the host's default libc may differ.

The [`tcache_poisoning/start`](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/glibc-chunk-poc-basic/blob/main/tcache_poisoning/start) script compiles with GCC debugging information, changes the libc dependency and interpreter using `patchelf`, then opens GDB. Its absolute `/home/llk/...` paths require local equivalents. The README also describes adding allocator source and debug information.

## Development history and notes

[Read the allocator notes and references](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/glibc-chunk-poc-basic/blob/main/README.md) · [Browse all examples](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/glibc-chunk-poc-basic/tree/main) · [View repository commits](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/glibc-chunk-poc-basic/commits/main/)

security-foundations/projects/redcortex.body:
## Team project

RedCortex is a CloudEver Team project developed collaboratively for authorized CTF, laboratory, and competition environments. Its architecture combines a fixed workflow graph with an Agent that chooses the next stage, specialist Agents, and persistent task memory in `topology.md` and per-node Markdown files. This portfolio record credits the collaborative team.

## Implementation and entry point

The repository includes a Python orchestration layer, a FastAPI interface, Docker/MCP sandbox integration, task-state persistence, and tests. The web interface exposes workflow state and task artifacts. See the [README](https://github.com/CloudEver-Team/RedCortex#readme) for architecture, prerequisites, and setup; it documents Python 3.12+ and scope controls for authorized assets.

The README notes that a top-level `LICENSE` file has not yet been provided.

[View source](https://github.com/CloudEver-Team/RedCortex)

meta.title: cs408-computer-networks
meta.excerpt: AtlasNet teaches computer networking through a persistent file service, reliable UDP transfers, packet encoding, and routing experiments.

software-foundations/computer-networks/c.body:
## Overview

AtlasNet connects 408 networking concepts to a working file-transfer system. Its Python implementation includes a TCP file service, authenticated uploads, persistent storage, and a custom reliable UDP protocol with retransmission, reordering, and whole-file integrity checks. Packet encoders produce standard-format PCAP files, while routing and transport models make protocol decisions inspectable.

## Start learning

With Python 3.11+, follow the [README](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-computer-networks#readme) to run the server and client in separate terminals. Start with a real upload/download, then introduce packet loss and compare the recovered file. The repository includes a staged Chinese course, original questions, and tests for protocol behavior and failure handling.

## Current scope

The file transfers use real sockets. Packet captures are synthesized, while routing, TCP control, and congestion behavior are explored through teaching models. The course maps these mechanisms to source files, experiments, and tests.

## Source

[GitHub repository](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-computer-networks)

meta.title: cs408-computer-organization
meta.excerpt: AtlasMachine connects computer-organization concepts through an assembler, instruction execution, a five-stage pipeline, caches, and device models.

software-foundations/computer-organizati.body:
## Overview

AtlasMachine is a Python teaching computer built around an assembler, executable instruction bytes, RAM, caches, a five-stage pipeline, and memory-mapped devices. Its statistics program reads input, computes results, and transfers them to a disk-image file, connecting data representation and CPU execution to observable outputs.

## Try the machine

Using Python 3.11+, run this command from the repository directory:

```console
python -m atlas run examples/statistics.s --input examples/numbers.txt --pipeline
```

The [README and course](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-computer-organization#readme) explain debugging, pipeline traces, numeric experiments, and original assessment questions. Source and tests expose the mechanisms behind the output.

## Current scope

The execution environment uses a documented subset of RISC-V instruction encodings with custom teaching devices. Pipeline timing treats cache accesses as one cycle. The topic map distinguishes implemented mechanisms from theory material.

## Source

[GitHub repository](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-computer-organization)

meta.title: cs408-data-structures
meta.excerpt: AtlasSearch puts data structures to work in a persistent local document search engine with Boolean queries, phrase matching, suggestions, and graph exploration.

software-foundations/data-structures/cs4.body:
## Overview

AtlasSearch is a local document-search engine that gives core data structures practical responsibilities. Inverted indexes support Boolean retrieval, KMP checks phrases, a Trie provides prefix suggestions, and an AVL tree supports document-length ranges. Graph algorithms explore document relationships, while Huffman coding and checked snapshots support backup and recovery.

## Search your own notes

With Python 3.11+, run these commands in the repository:

```console
python -m atlas_search --db .atlas init
python -m atlas_search --db .atlas index examples/corpus
python -m atlas_search --db .atlas search "tree AND NOT graph"
```

Replace the sample corpus with your own UTF-8 notes. The [README](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-data-structures#readme) links the course, original exercises, algorithm implementations, and verification commands.

## Current scope

The engine persists documents and indexes, with integrity checks and recovery behavior. Tokenization and ranking follow explicit teaching rules. The course topic map separates implemented algorithms from theory material.

## Source

[GitHub repository](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-data-structures)

meta.title: cs408-operating-systems
meta.excerpt: AtlasOS teaches operating-system mechanisms through executable programs, scheduling, blocking IPC, paging, persistent files, and restartable checkpoints.

software-foundations/operating-systems/c.body:
## Overview

AtlasOS is a user-space teaching kernel implemented in Python. Programs pass through an interpreter and process scheduler, interact through blocking pipes, access paged memory, and save files in an inode-based teaching filesystem. Checkpoints preserve execution state across separate host processes, making scheduling and persistence observable throughout a complete workflow.

## Run a complete workflow

With Python 3.11+, execute these commands in the repository:

```console
python -m atlasos --home .atlasos install-examples
python -m atlasos --home .atlasos run /programs/pipeline.atl
python -m atlasos --home .atlasos cat /sum.txt
```

The producer/consumer example writes its calculated result into the teaching filesystem. The [course and README](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-operating-systems#readme) cover scheduling, synchronization, memory, storage, original questions, and failure-recovery tests.

## Current scope

Files and checkpoints persist on the host, while CPU privilege, page frames, interrupts, and disk tracks are explicit models. The course explains these boundaries and maps implemented mechanisms and theory topics to the source.

## Source

[GitHub repository](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/cs408-operating-systems)

meta.title: llkchatroom
meta.excerpt: An Android chat client and Java socket server for text and file exchange on a local network. Separate connections handle messages and binary transfers.

software-foundations/projects/llkchatroo.body:
## Background

A small chat application makes network programming tangible: a user action becomes a message, a server forwards it, and another device updates its interface. llkchatroom explores that path through an Android client and a Java server, including text and file exchange over a local network.

The repository contains the Android application under `app/`, the socket server under `server/`, and a README explaining the communication flow with code examples.

## Implementation

The server opens two TCP listeners: port `8848` for messages and port `18848` for file transfers. Each accepted connection is assigned a worker thread. The message worker reads text lines and forwards them to connected message clients; the file worker receives file metadata and bytes, stores the transfer, and relays it to file clients.

On Android, `ClientThread` and `FileThread` manage the two connections. Handlers and Loopers carry work between the interface and network threads, while a RecyclerView displays sent and received messages. The login screen records a display name and the device's local address. Text records include those fields alongside the message content.

File transfers use a separate path with a filename, a declared length, byte-stream operations, and an end marker. Pictures, video, and audio travel through this generic file mechanism. The implementation provides a compact case study in message framing, connection handling, and coordinating network work with an Android interface.

## Inspect the work

- [Android client](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkchatroom/tree/main/app/src/main/java/com/example/chatroom): activities, message model, adapter, and socket threads.
- [Server implementation](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkchatroom/tree/main/server): listeners and message/file relay workers.
- [Protocol walkthrough](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkchatroom/blob/main/README.md): setup steps and explanations of the client/server code.
- [Development history](https://github.com/Y0uYuGe/llkchatroom/commits/main/): changes recorded in the repository.

## Running the project

Use Android Studio and the repository's Gradle project for the client, plus a Java environment for the server. The checked-in Android configuration uses compile/target SDK `34` and minimum SDK `21`.

Start the server on a reachable computer, set the server address in both Android connection classes, and place the devices on the same network. Adjust the server's file-storage path for the host machine and permit access to the two listening ports. The README describes a phone-and-computer hotspot setup for trying the application.
